title: Docker: What Actually Happens?
description: Test what Docker does with build contexts, caching, image layers, multi-stage builds, Unix signals, networking, storage, and Linux isolation. Each Question asks you to reason through a concrete situation.

questions.title: Can `COPY` reach a sibling directory outside the build context?
questions.description: The project is `/work/app`, a secret is `/work/private-key`, and the build runs as `docker build /work/app`. The Dockerfile contains `COPY ../private-key /run/private-key`.

options.text: Yes. `COPY` resolves paths relative to the Dockerfile on the client
No. The builder can read only the selected build context or a named context
Yes, but only when the destination is under `/run`
No. `COPY` can copy only files tracked by Git

questions.explanation: `docker build /work/app` makes `/work/app` the default context. Docker cannot read `/work/private-key` from there. BuildKit strips leading `../` segments instead of letting `COPY` escape the context. To use another directory, pass it as a named context.
questions.references:
[Docker Docs: Build context](https://docs.docker.com/build/concepts/context/)

[Docker Docs: `docker image build`: accessing paths outside the context](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/image/build/#accessing-paths-outside-the-build-context)

questions.title: What happens when `.dockerignore` excludes a file that `COPY` requests?
questions.description: `.dockerignore` contains `secrets.env`, while the Dockerfile contains `COPY secrets.env /app/secrets.env`.

options.text: The file is sent to the builder but omitted from the final image
The file is replaced with an empty file so the build can continue
The file is removed from the context before transfer, so `COPY` fails because the source is missing
The ignore rule affects `ADD` but not `COPY`

questions.explanation: Docker removes ignored files before sending the context to the builder. `secrets.env` never arrives, so `COPY` cannot find it and the build fails. `.dockerignore` can keep a secret out of the context, but an ignored file cannot also be copied.

questions.title: Which ignore file controls a build when both applicable files exist?
questions.description: The context root has `.dockerignore`. A build using `docker/build.Dockerfile` also has `docker/build.Dockerfile.dockerignore` beside that Dockerfile.

options.text: Docker merges both files, with the root file evaluated last
The Dockerfile-specific `build.Dockerfile.dockerignore` takes precedence
Only the root `.dockerignore` is recognized
Whichever file has the newer modification time wins

questions.explanation: Docker can use an ignore file named after a specific Dockerfile and placed beside it. If that file exists, it takes precedence over the root `.dockerignore`. This lets different builds use different ignore rules.

questions.title: Why does `COPY main.c /src/` fail when the Dockerfile is piped as the build context?
questions.description: The command is `docker build - < Dockerfile`, and `main.c` exists in the current client directory.

options.text: A text-file context has no filesystem context, so local files such as `main.c` are unavailable
Standard input builds prohibit every `COPY`, including `--from` copies
The `-` argument selects the root directory `/` as context
Docker requires the source file to be executable when using standard input

questions.explanation: Here, `-` supplies a text-file context, not the current directory. Docker reads the text as a Dockerfile and provides no filesystem context. The builder therefore cannot see `main.c`, even though the file exists on the client.

questions.title: Does touching a copied file invalidate its build cache?
questions.description: `app.js` has identical content, permissions, ownership, and size, but its modification time changes before rebuilding `COPY app.js /app/app.js`.

images.alt: Two Dockerfiles side by side. Source first — FROM, COPY . /app, RUN npm ci — invalidates the COPY layer on any file edit and every layer above it, so the install reruns on every build. Dependencies first — FROM, COPY package*.json, RUN npm ci, then COPY . /app — confines a source edit to the last layer and keeps the install cached until a manifest changes. Four cards follow: a COPY's cache key is the file's content plus metadata such as mode and ownership, so changing only its modification time invalidates nothing; a RUN's cache key is the command string alone, so a lone apt-get update matches last week's and reuses a stale index; --mount=type=secret keeps the value out of both the image and the cache key, which also means rotating a secret does not invalidate that step; and --mount=type=cache needs BuildKit and never becomes part of the image.
images.caption: Content and metadata — not the modification time on its own.

options.text: Yes. Any newer modification time forces `COPY` and all later instructions to run
No. Docker leaves modification time out of the cache checksum
Only if the modification time changes by more than one second
Only remote builders ignore modification time

questions.explanation: For `ADD`, `COPY`, and `RUN` bind mounts, Docker builds a checksum from file metadata. It leaves out `mtime`. If only the modification time changed, the cache entry remains valid. A content change or other relevant metadata change can still invalidate it.

questions.title: Which changes can invalidate the cache for `COPY package.json /app/`?
questions.description: Select every change that can affect Docker's checksum for this file.

images.alt: Two Dockerfiles side by side. Source first — FROM, COPY . /app, RUN npm ci — invalidates the COPY layer on any file edit and every layer above it, so the install reruns on every build. Dependencies first — FROM, COPY package*.json, RUN npm ci, then COPY . /app — confines a source edit to the last layer and keeps the install cached until a manifest changes. Four cards follow: a COPY's cache key is the file's content plus metadata such as mode and ownership, so changing only its modification time invalidates nothing; a RUN's cache key is the command string alone, so a lone apt-get update matches last week's and reuses a stale index; --mount=type=secret keeps the value out of both the image and the cache key, which also means rotating a secret does not invalidate that step; and --mount=type=cache needs BuildKit and never becomes part of the image.
images.caption: The `COPY` card lists exactly what counts.

options.text: Changing the contents of `package.json`
Changing relevant file metadata such as its permissions
Changing only the file's modification time
Changing a file excluded by `.dockerignore` and not used by the instruction

questions.explanation: Docker checks the files used by `COPY`. Changes to content or metadata such as permissions can change the checksum, but a modification-time change alone cannot. An ignored, unrelated file has no effect because the builder never receives it.
questions.references:
[Docker Docs: Build cache invalidation](https://docs.docker.com/build/cache/invalidation/)

[Docker Docs: Using the build cache](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/building-images/using-the-build-cache/)

questions.title: Why can `RUN apt-get update` return week-old data during a rebuild?

images.alt: Two Dockerfiles side by side. Source first — FROM, COPY . /app, RUN npm ci — invalidates the COPY layer on any file edit and every layer above it, so the install reruns on every build. Dependencies first — FROM, COPY package*.json, RUN npm ci, then COPY . /app — confines a source edit to the last layer and keeps the install cached until a manifest changes. Four cards follow: a COPY's cache key is the file's content plus metadata such as mode and ownership, so changing only its modification time invalidates nothing; a RUN's cache key is the command string alone, so a lone apt-get update matches last week's and reuses a stale index; --mount=type=secret keeps the value out of both the image and the cache key, which also means rotating a secret does not invalidate that step; and --mount=type=cache needs BuildKit and never becomes part of the image.
images.caption: The command string is the whole key, so the same string hits.

options.text: Docker checks the package repository only when the base image tag changes
Docker reuses the cached `RUN` result without checking whether remote package data changed
Docker freezes network access for all cached Dockerfiles
Package managers automatically restore their index to the image creation date

questions.explanation: Docker does not contact the package repository while checking this cache entry. If the command and earlier layers still match, Docker can reuse the old result. Use `--no-cache`, `--no-cache-filter`, or a changed earlier layer when the step must run again.

questions.title: Which Dockerfile order keeps the dependency cache when application source changes?
questions.description: Assume a Node project whose dependencies are determined by `package.json` and `package-lock.json`.

images.alt: Two Dockerfiles side by side. Source first — FROM, COPY . /app, RUN npm ci — invalidates the COPY layer on any file edit and every layer above it, so the install reruns on every build. Dependencies first — FROM, COPY package*.json, RUN npm ci, then COPY . /app — confines a source edit to the last layer and keeps the install cached until a manifest changes. Four cards follow: a COPY's cache key is the file's content plus metadata such as mode and ownership, so changing only its modification time invalidates nothing; a RUN's cache key is the command string alone, so a lone apt-get update matches last week's and reuses a stale index; --mount=type=secret keeps the value out of both the image and the cache key, which also means rotating a secret does not invalidate that step; and --mount=type=cache needs BuildKit and never becomes part of the image.
images.caption: The green Dockerfile: manifests before source.

options.text: Copy all source, install dependencies, then copy the manifests again
Copy the manifests, install dependencies, then copy the frequently changing source
Install dependencies before copying any manifests
Copy source and manifests in separate instructions after dependency installation

questions.explanation: Once a layer changes, later cache entries are invalid. Copy the package files and install dependencies before copying the source. A source edit then rebuilds only the later layers, while a dependency change still reruns the install step.
questions.references: [Docker Docs: Optimize cache usage: order your layers](https://docs.docker.com/build/cache/optimize/#order-your-layers)

questions.title: What must be true of a build that uses `RUN --mount=type=cache`?
questions.description: A package manager uses a cache mount to retain downloaded packages between builds.

images.alt: Two Dockerfiles side by side. Source first — FROM, COPY . /app, RUN npm ci — invalidates the COPY layer on any file edit and every layer above it, so the install reruns on every build. Dependencies first — FROM, COPY package*.json, RUN npm ci, then COPY . /app — confines a source edit to the last layer and keeps the install cached until a manifest changes. Four cards follow: a COPY's cache key is the file's content plus metadata such as mode and ownership, so changing only its modification time invalidates nothing; a RUN's cache key is the command string alone, so a lone apt-get update matches last week's and reuses a stale index; --mount=type=secret keeps the value out of both the image and the cache key, which also means rotating a secret does not invalidate that step; and --mount=type=cache needs BuildKit and never becomes part of the image.
images.caption: BuildKit only, and never part of the image.

options.text: The final image will contain the cache directory exactly as the build saw it
The build must work with any cache contents, including an empty cache
Every build receives an immutable snapshot of the cache
A cache mount can be read only by the build that created it

questions.explanation: A cache mount saves reusable downloads between builds, but Docker may overwrite or garbage-collect its contents. The build must work with an empty or unexpected cache. Files in the cache mount do not become normal output of the `RUN` layer.
questions.references:
[Docker Docs: Optimize cache usage: cache mounts](https://docs.docker.com/build/cache/optimize/#use-cache-mounts)

[Docker Docs: Dockerfile reference: `RUN --mount=type=cache`](https://docs.docker.com/reference/dockerfile/#run---mounttypecache)

questions.title: How should you pass a private registry token to one build step?

images.alt: Two Dockerfiles side by side. Source first — FROM, COPY . /app, RUN npm ci — invalidates the COPY layer on any file edit and every layer above it, so the install reruns on every build. Dependencies first — FROM, COPY package*.json, RUN npm ci, then COPY . /app — confines a source edit to the last layer and keeps the install cached until a manifest changes. Four cards follow: a COPY's cache key is the file's content plus metadata such as mode and ownership, so changing only its modification time invalidates nothing; a RUN's cache key is the command string alone, so a lone apt-get update matches last week's and reuses a stale index; --mount=type=secret keeps the value out of both the image and the cache key, which also means rotating a secret does not invalidate that step; and --mount=type=cache needs BuildKit and never becomes part of the image.
images.caption: The secret mount is the one that leaves nothing behind.

options.text: Declare it with `ARG TOKEN` and pass `--build-arg TOKEN=...`
Declare it with `ENV TOKEN=...` and unset it in a later layer
Pass it with `docker build --secret` and consume it using `RUN --mount=type=secret`
Copy it into the image and delete it before `CMD`

questions.explanation: `ARG` and `ENV` can leave a secret in the final image, its metadata, or its history. A secret mount exposes the token only while that `RUN` step executes. The normal image layer does not contain the mounted secret.

questions.title: Does rotating a build secret automatically invalidate the consuming `RUN` cache?

images.alt: Two Dockerfiles side by side. Source first — FROM, COPY . /app, RUN npm ci — invalidates the COPY layer on any file edit and every layer above it, so the install reruns on every build. Dependencies first — FROM, COPY package*.json, RUN npm ci, then COPY . /app — confines a source edit to the last layer and keeps the install cached until a manifest changes. Four cards follow: a COPY's cache key is the file's content plus metadata such as mode and ownership, so changing only its modification time invalidates nothing; a RUN's cache key is the command string alone, so a lone apt-get update matches last week's and reuses a stale index; --mount=type=secret keeps the value out of both the image and the cache key, which also means rotating a secret does not invalidate that step; and --mount=type=cache needs BuildKit and never becomes part of the image.
images.caption: Outside the image, and outside the cache key too.

options.text: Yes. Secret contents always become part of the layer checksum
No. Docker ignores the secret value but includes the secret ID and mount path
Only secrets longer than 32 bytes invalidate the cache
No. Neither the secret value nor its mount settings can ever affect caching

questions.explanation: Docker does not include a secret's value in the cache checksum, so rotating the value alone can still produce a cache hit. The secret ID and mount path do affect the checksum. If rotation must rerun the step, change a separate build argument as a cache buster.

questions.title: Which build-stage files end up in the final image?
questions.description: A `build` stage contains a compiler, source tree, package cache, and `/out/server`. A fresh runtime stage contains `COPY --from=build /out/server /server`.

options.text: Every build-stage layer plus a marker hiding the compiler
Only the runtime stage's base and files added to that stage, such as `/server`
The compiler and source tree, but not the package cache
Nothing from the build stage because stages cannot exchange files

questions.explanation: Each `FROM` starts a new stage. The runtime stage receives only what its own instructions add, including `/server` from `COPY --from=build`. The compiler, source tree, and package cache stay in the build stage.

questions.title: Which image does `docker build --target test .` produce?

options.text: An image from the named `test` stage instead of continuing to the Dockerfile's final stage
Only the individual instruction labeled `test`
The final image, with tests disabled
All stages merged into a single filesystem

questions.explanation: `--target test` makes the named `test` stage the output. BuildKit builds that stage and its dependencies, but it can skip unrelated earlier stages. This lets one Dockerfile provide separate test, debug, and runtime images.
questions.references:
[Docker Docs: Stop at a specific build stage](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/#stop-at-a-specific-build-stage)

[Docker Docs: BuildKit stage dependency differences](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/#differences-between-legacy-builder-and-buildkit)

questions.title: Why can deleting a 200 MB archive in a later `RUN` leave the image roughly 200 MB larger?
questions.description: The Dockerfile downloads `/tmp/sdk.tar` in one `RUN` instruction and deletes it in a later `RUN` instruction.

images.alt: A stack of read-only image layers — FROM node:22-slim, COPY package.json, RUN npm ci, COPY . /app — with one thin read-write container layer on top, unique to that container. Notes explain that writing a file that came from the image copies it up into the top layer first while the layer beneath is untouched; that changing one byte of a huge file makes OverlayFS copy the whole file up before the write; that deleting something in a later RUN leaves the earlier layer carrying the bytes and only records a whiteout; and that removing the container removes the writable layer with it. Three cards then cover what survives instead: a named volume, which outlives its container and is seeded from the image directory when empty; a bind mount, where the host path hides whatever the image had there and is read-write by default; and a tmpfs mount, which lives in host memory and vanishes when the container stops.
images.caption: A whiteout hides the bytes; it does not remove them.

options.text: The delete changes the visible filesystem, but the archive's bytes remain in the earlier immutable layer
Docker compresses deleted files only after the container starts
Files under `/tmp` always count twice in image size
`RUN rm` changes image metadata but never the filesystem

questions.explanation: Image layers are immutable. The later deletion hides the archive in the combined filesystem, but its bytes remain in the earlier layer and still count toward image size. Create and remove temporary data in one layer, or keep the work in a build stage that the final image does not use.

questions.title: Where does a running container write `/etc/app.conf` when the file came from its image?

images.alt: A stack of read-only image layers — FROM node:22-slim, COPY package.json, RUN npm ci, COPY . /app — with one thin read-write container layer on top, unique to that container. Notes explain that writing a file that came from the image copies it up into the top layer first while the layer beneath is untouched; that changing one byte of a huge file makes OverlayFS copy the whole file up before the write; that deleting something in a later RUN leaves the earlier layer carrying the bytes and only records a whiteout; and that removing the container removes the writable layer with it. Three cards then cover what survives instead: a named volume, which outlives its container and is seeded from the image directory when empty; a bind mount, where the host path hides whatever the image had there and is read-write by default; and a tmpfs mount, which lives in host memory and vanishes when the container stops.
images.caption: Copied up into the top layer; the image layer is untouched.

options.text: Directly into the image's newest read-only layer
Into that container's thin writable layer, leaving the shared image layers unchanged
Into every container created from the same image
Into a Docker volume that is created automatically for every path

questions.explanation: Docker puts a writable layer on top of the image for each container. The change goes into that layer, so other containers still see the image's original file. Docker removes the writable layer when it removes the container.
questions.references:
[Docker Docs: Understanding image layers](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/building-images/understanding-image-layers/)

[Docker Docs: Storage drivers: containers and layers](https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/#container-and-layers)

questions.title: What can happen when an OverlayFS-backed container changes one byte in a large image file for the first time?

images.alt: A stack of read-only image layers — FROM node:22-slim, COPY package.json, RUN npm ci, COPY . /app — with one thin read-write container layer on top, unique to that container. Notes explain that writing a file that came from the image copies it up into the top layer first while the layer beneath is untouched; that changing one byte of a huge file makes OverlayFS copy the whole file up before the write; that deleting something in a later RUN leaves the earlier layer carrying the bytes and only records a whiteout; and that removing the container removes the writable layer with it. Three cards then cover what survives instead: a named volume, which outlives its container and is seeded from the image directory when empty; a bind mount, where the host path hides whatever the image had there and is read-write by default; and a tmpfs mount, which lives in host memory and vanishes when the container stops.
images.caption: Copy-up is per file, not per byte.

options.text: OverlayFS copies the whole file into the writable layer before modifying the copy
Only the changed byte is stored, because OverlayFS always copies at block granularity
The lower image layer becomes writable for that container
The change is rejected unless the file is on a named volume

questions.explanation: With the `overlay2` storage driver, the first write triggers `copy_up`. OverlayFS copies the whole file into the writable layer and changes that copy. It works at file level, so a one-byte edit can copy a large file. Later writes use the copied file.
questions.references: [Docker Docs: OverlayFS: writing to a file for the first time](https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/overlayfs-driver/#writing-to-a-file-for-the-first-time)

questions.title: Which image reference guarantees the same published image content on later pulls?

options.text: `ubuntu:latest`
`ubuntu:24.04`
`ubuntu@sha256:<exact-digest>`
`ubuntu` without a tag

questions.explanation: A publisher can move a tag to a newer image. A digest identifies exact content, so pulling by digest gives you the same published image each time. You must update the digest yourself to receive a newer image or security fixes.

questions.title: Why might `ENTRYPOINT node server.js` hide Docker's stop signal from Node?

options.text: Shell form runs through `/bin/sh -c`, so the shell can remain PID 1 instead of replacing itself with Node
Node processes cannot receive Unix signals in containers
`ENTRYPOINT` disables signals unless an `EXPOSE` instruction is present
Docker sends stop signals only to programs started by `CMD`

questions.explanation: Shell form runs through `/bin/sh -c`, so the shell can become PID 1 while Node runs as its child. The shell may not forward Docker's signal. Exec form, `ENTRYPOINT ["node", "server.js"]`, starts Node as the main process. A wrapper script must forward signals and use `exec` when it hands control to the application.

questions.title: What does `docker stop` do when the main process does not exit during its grace period?

options.text: It pauses the container indefinitely
It sends the configured stop signal (normally `SIGTERM`), waits, then forcibly sends `SIGKILL`
It immediately sends `SIGKILL` and never waits
It sends `SIGINT` repeatedly until every process exits

questions.explanation: Docker sends the configured stop signal to the main process. The default is `SIGTERM`. If the process is still running after the timeout, Docker sends `SIGKILL`, which the process cannot catch for cleanup. `STOPSIGNAL`, `--stop-signal`, and timeout settings can change the graceful phase.

questions.title: By default, how many seconds does Docker wait before killing an unresponsive Linux container?
questions.description: Assume neither the container nor the command configures a different stop timeout. Enter the number of seconds.
questions.explanation: Docker waits 10 seconds by default for a Linux container and 30 seconds for a Windows container. It then sends `SIGKILL` if the process is still running. A timeout of `-1` tells Docker to wait without a deadline.

questions.title: Why would you use `docker run --init`?

options.text: It inserts a small PID 1 that forwards signals and reaps zombie processes
It rebuilds the image before every container start
It grants the container a private kernel
It waits for every declared network port to become healthy

questions.explanation: PID 1 has special process-management duties on Linux. `--init` inserts a small init process, backed by `tini` in Docker's default installation, that reaps zombie processes. Docker's Compose documentation also states that the init process forwards signals.

questions.title: What does `EXPOSE 8080` do by itself?

options.text: It opens host port 8080 to the public internet
It records container port 8080 in the image but does not publish a host port
It forces the application to listen on port 8080
It creates a user-defined bridge network named `8080`

questions.explanation: `EXPOSE` records the port that the image expects the application to use. It does not start a listener or create a host mapping. Use `-p` for a chosen mapping, or `-P` to publish every exposed port to an ephemeral host port.

questions.title: Where does traffic to host port 8080 go with `docker run -p 8080:80 nginx`?

options.text: To TCP port 80 inside the container
To TCP port 8080 inside the container
To host port 80 after passing through container port 8080
Nowhere unless the Dockerfile also says `EXPOSE 8080`

questions.explanation: The syntax is `HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT`. Docker forwards connections from host port 8080 to TCP port 80 in the container. An explicit `-p` mapping works even if the Dockerfile has no matching `EXPOSE` instruction.

questions.title: Who can potentially reach `-p 8080:80` when no host IP is specified?

options.text: Only processes inside the Docker host
Anyone who can reach a host network interface, subject to firewall and routing
Only containers on the same bridge
Only the user who launched the container

questions.explanation: Docker publishes on all host addresses when you omit the host IP, so another machine may be able to reach the port. Bind to loopback, such as `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80`, when only the Docker host should connect. Add the equivalent IPv6 loopback mapping if needed.

questions.title: How should `web` connect to `db` on the same user-defined bridge?

options.text: Use `db` as the hostname and the database's container port
Use `localhost` because both containers share loopback
Use the Docker host's published database port in every case
Read the database container's IP once and hard-code it

questions.explanation: A user-defined bridge provides DNS by container name or alias. `web` can connect to `db` at the database's container port without publishing that port on the host. Unlike a hard-coded IP address, the name still works after Docker recreates the container with a new address.

questions.title: What does `localhost` mean inside the `web` container?
questions.description: A database runs in a separate `db` container on the same user-defined network.

options.text: The `web` container's own loopback interface
The Docker host
Whichever container started most recently
Every container attached to the bridge

questions.explanation: Each container has its own network stack and loopback interface. Inside `web`, `localhost` points back to `web`, not to `db` or the Docker host. Use the hostname `db` to reach the database on this network.

questions.title: Must a database port be published for a peer on the same user-defined bridge to reach it?
questions.description: Assume the database listens on its container network interface.

options.text: Yes. Every container-to-container connection must go through a host port
No. Containers on the same user-defined bridge can connect directly
Yes, unless both containers use the same image
No, but only ports named by `EXPOSE` are reachable between peers

questions.explanation: Containers on the same user-defined bridge can connect directly to one another's ports. Publishing makes a port available through the host or, under the default bridge rules, to other networks. It is not needed for peers on the same network. `EXPOSE` does not filter this traffic.

questions.title: What happens to a named volume after the container using it is removed?

images.alt: A stack of read-only image layers — FROM node:22-slim, COPY package.json, RUN npm ci, COPY . /app — with one thin read-write container layer on top, unique to that container. Notes explain that writing a file that came from the image copies it up into the top layer first while the layer beneath is untouched; that changing one byte of a huge file makes OverlayFS copy the whole file up before the write; that deleting something in a later RUN leaves the earlier layer carrying the bytes and only records a whiteout; and that removing the container removes the writable layer with it. Three cards then cover what survives instead: a named volume, which outlives its container and is seeded from the image directory when empty; a bind mount, where the host path hides whatever the image had there and is read-write by default; and a tmpfs mount, which lives in host memory and vanishes when the container stops.
images.caption: The left-hand card: the volume outlives its container.

options.text: It persists independently until the volume itself is removed
It is copied back into the image
It is always deleted with the container
It survives only while another container is running

questions.explanation: A volume has its own lifecycle. Removing a container does not remove a named volume, even if the removal command also cleans up attached anonymous volumes. A replacement container can mount the same named volume and read its data.

questions.title: What initially appears in a new empty volume mounted over a non-empty image directory?
questions.description: The image contains `/app/defaults/config.ini`. A newly created empty volume is mounted at `/app/defaults` with default volume behavior.

images.alt: A stack of read-only image layers — FROM node:22-slim, COPY package.json, RUN npm ci, COPY . /app — with one thin read-write container layer on top, unique to that container. Notes explain that writing a file that came from the image copies it up into the top layer first while the layer beneath is untouched; that changing one byte of a huge file makes OverlayFS copy the whole file up before the write; that deleting something in a later RUN leaves the earlier layer carrying the bytes and only records a whiteout; and that removing the container removes the writable layer with it. Three cards then cover what survives instead: a named volume, which outlives its container and is seeded from the image directory when empty; a bind mount, where the host path hides whatever the image had there and is read-write by default; and a tmpfs mount, which lives in host memory and vanishes when the container stops.
images.caption: An empty volume is seeded from the directory it covers.

options.text: The image's existing files are copied into the empty volume, so `config.ini` appears there
The directory is always empty because every mount discards image content
The volume contains a symbolic link to the image layer
Container creation fails because the target directory is non-empty

questions.explanation: By default, Docker copies files already at the mount target into a new empty volume. In this case, the volume receives `config.ini`. Use `volume-nocopy` when the volume should remain empty.
questions.references: [Docker Docs: Mounting a volume over existing data](https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/volumes/#mounting-a-volume-over-existing-data)

questions.title: What does a default read-write bind mount over `/app` do?
questions.description: The image already has files in `/app`, and the host directory `/work/source` is mounted there. Select every correct statement.

Notes explain that writing a file that came from the image copies it up into the top layer first while the layer beneath is untouched; that changing one byte of a huge file makes OverlayFS copy the whole file up before the write; that deleting something in a later RUN leaves the earlier layer carrying the bytes and only records a whiteout; and that removing the container removes the writable layer with it. Three cards then cover what survives instead: a named volume, which outlives its container and is seeded from the image directory when empty; a bind mount, where the host path hides whatever the image had there and is read-write by default; and a tmpfs mount, which lives in host memory and vanishes when the container stops.
images.caption: The host path wins for as long as it is mounted.

options.text: The image's pre-existing `/app` files are obscured while the mount is present
Container processes can modify files in `/work/source` because bind mounts are writable by default
The image's hidden `/app` files are permanently deleted from its layers
Docker copies `/work/source` into a daemon-managed volume before the container starts

questions.explanation: The bind mount covers the image's `/app` files while the mount exists, but it does not delete them from the image. Bind mounts are writable by default, so the container can change files in `/work/source` on the host. Use `readonly` or `ro` when the container needs only read access.

questions.title: What happens to files in a Docker `tmpfs` mount when the container stops?

images.alt: A stack of read-only image layers — FROM node:22-slim, COPY package.json, RUN npm ci, COPY . /app — with one thin read-write container layer on top, unique to that container. Notes explain that writing a file that came from the image copies it up into the top layer first while the layer beneath is untouched; that changing one byte of a huge file makes OverlayFS copy the whole file up before the write; that deleting something in a later RUN leaves the earlier layer carrying the bytes and only records a whiteout; and that removing the container removes the writable layer with it. Three cards then cover what survives instead: a named volume, which outlives its container and is seeded from the image directory when empty; a bind mount, where the host path hides whatever the image had there and is read-write by default; and a tmpfs mount, which lives in host memory and vanishes when the container stops.
images.caption: Memory only, and gone on stop.

options.text: They are committed into a new image layer
They are removed with the temporary mount and do not persist as container storage
They move automatically into a named volume
They remain in host RAM until Docker is uninstalled

questions.explanation: Docker removes a `tmpfs` mount when the container stops, so its files do not persist as container storage. The data normally lives in host memory instead of the container's writable layer. Linux may still write tmpfs pages to swap, so `tmpfs` is not a guarantee that bytes never touch disk.

questions.title: What happens to database files written only into a container's writable layer after that container is deleted?

Notes explain that writing a file that came from the image copies it up into the top layer first while the layer beneath is untouched; that changing one byte of a huge file makes OverlayFS copy the whole file up before the write; that deleting something in a later RUN leaves the earlier layer carrying the bytes and only records a whiteout; and that removing the container removes the writable layer with it. Three cards then cover what survives instead: a named volume, which outlives its container and is seeded from the image directory when empty; a bind mount, where the host path hides whatever the image had there and is read-write by default; and a tmpfs mount, which lives in host memory and vanishes when the container stops.
images.caption: The top layer dies with the container.

options.text: They are available to the next container using the same image tag
They are lost with the deleted container's writable layer
They are pushed to the registry with the image
They become an anonymous volume automatically

questions.explanation: The writable layer belongs to one container. Stopping the container keeps that layer, but deleting the container removes it. Put durable or write-heavy data in a volume or another storage system.

questions.title: Which statements accurately describe default Linux container isolation?
questions.description: Select every correct statement for ordinary Docker Engine containers, not Docker Desktop's additional VM boundary.

options.text: Namespaces separate views of resources such as processes and networks
Containers share the host's Linux kernel rather than booting a private kernel per container
A container is automatically safe to treat as a hardware virtual machine boundary
Root inside a container always has unrestricted root access to the host

questions.explanation: Namespaces give a container separate views of resources such as processes and networks. Cgroups account for and limit resources. Containers still use the host kernel, while capabilities and seccomp reduce what their processes may do. The strength of the boundary depends on the container configuration and the host kernel; it is not the same as a VM with its own kernel.
questions.references:
[Docker Docs: Docker Engine security](https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/)

[Docker Docs: Isolation layers: containers share the host kernel](https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes/security/isolation/)

questions.title: Without resource limits, how much CPU and memory can a container use?

options.text: At most one CPU and 512 MB of memory
As much as the host kernel scheduler and available resources allow
An equal hard partition of the host for each running container
No CPU until `--cpus` and no memory until `--memory` are supplied

questions.explanation: Docker does not set a hard CPU or memory limit by default. A container can use as much as the host kernel allows, which can starve other workloads or trigger out-of-memory handling. Use flags such as `--cpus` and `--memory` to set cgroup limits.

questions.title: With these limits, how many megabytes of swap can the container use?
questions.description: The container starts with `--memory=300m --memory-swap=600m`. Enter only the swap amount in megabytes.
questions.explanation: `--memory-swap` sets the combined RAM and swap allowance. Subtract the 300 MB RAM limit from the 600 MB combined limit: `600 - 300 = 300`. The container may use 300 MB of swap.

questions.title: What does Docker's default seccomp profile do on a supported Linux host?

options.text: It filters selected system calls to reduce the kernel attack surface while allowing common workloads
It gives each container a separate Linux kernel
It encrypts all container filesystem layers
It publishes only ports named by `EXPOSE`

questions.explanation: Seccomp is a Linux kernel feature that restricts system calls. Docker uses a default profile when the host supports it, unless you override that profile. Seccomp works alongside namespaces, capabilities, cgroups, and other controls; it does not give the container a private kernel.
